newsitem.title: UK: Lead hits one-month high, backwardation erupts.
newsitem.headline: Lead hits one-month high, backwardation erupts.

text.p: Lead prices leapt to their for a month on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Friday, a sudden move that took place with the market snapping into backwardation.
Three months prices hit a high of $700 a tonne, up $25 from Thursday's $675 kerb close, but some $40 above the levels the market had languished at most of the week.
Traders said the viciousness of the move into backwardation was due to April date tightness, fund covering, and related buying against options.
"It is a very technical thing. Lead is a naturally hedge-short market, and it catches people out," one said.
The benchmark cash/threes spread was indicated at $16/17 backwardation on Friday, having been flat on Thursday evening. At the start of the week a $7 contango prevailed.
Tightness is centred around April, with April for two-weeks said to be trading at an $18 backwardation.
Fundamentally, nothing has emerged in the last 24 hours to justify the market's strength, with lead now approaching a flat period of the year for consumption, traders noted.
"We had been expecting prices to move higher during the first quarter, but the longer it went on the less likely it would happen," Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME trader Billiton Metals said.
"The battery season is at an end, and seasonally demand is weakening ahead of the summer period," he added.
Traders said the flare-up in technical tightness was typical of the lead market, where contangos are usual most of the time and trade hedgers will be sellers.
Investment funds, who have been prominent in all the metal markets recently, were said to be short of the April dates, and thus had to cover overnight.
There was also talk of nearby options being granted this week at strikes of $700 and $725, and with March being declared next week delta hedging fuelled the gains, traders said.
"All-in-all, there was a combination of factors which caught the market out," another trader said.
LME shorts also face problems if Exchange inventories are tightly-held or located in awkward locations, as could well be the case at present, analysts noted.
On Friday, LME stocks fell 225 tonnes to 108,250 tonnes, but 80,600 tonnes are in the Swedish delivery point of Helsingborg.
"I takes time to get at that metal," MacMillan noted. --London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
